body_text: Google dropped its annual Halloween “ Frightgeist ” data earlier today, revealing the costumes, candy, decor, and more that have spiked in popularity this year. Unsurprisingly, this year’s movies are playing a big part in the trending outfits of 2026, with Agamemnon from “The Odyssey” in fourth; Nikki from “Obsession” in third; and Buddy the Unicorn, the titular character from the viral horror phenomenon “Buddy,” taking first. The highest trending kids’ costumes this year have gone in a different direction, however, with the top two spots taken by country stars: apparently you can expect to greet swarms of younger trick-or-treaters dressed as Ella Langley and the late Dolly Parton this October 31. Never mind that it’s yet another screen to add to your roster! Never mind that “iPad” might just have been the perfect name for an Apple home hub had it not been taken in 2010! Just be happy that you now have a new option in the crowded market of big tech smart-home products to choose from, after Apple unveiled its HomeView smart display yesterday. Dubbed a “new way to enjoy entertainment, stay connected, and manage the home,” the 7-inch, $299 device will officially drop on Friday, November 13, per the company’s announcement . From the chaotic three-minute trailer, users will be able to play music, control smart devices, FaceTime hands-free, and access Siri AI — basically everything you can do from any number of the smaller Apple devices you already own, cementing the pithy “ It’s an iPhone for your home .” verdict from The Verge’s Jennifer Pattison Tuohy. Alongside another device to take to battle against Google and Amazon equivalents, Apple also announced new HomePod smart speakers, a fourth-generation Apple TV 4K, and a suite of smart-home accessories made in collaboration with LG. Increasing its offering of devices to dot around the house makes sense when taking a look at its Apple’s Wearables, Home and Accessories segment more broadly. The division that covers AirPods, Watches, TVs, Beats, and accessories like chargers and cases has seen revenues sink a little in recent years, with sales down some $3.2 billion in the first quarter of the year compared to their 2022 peak. It’s important to note that even with the declines more broadly, Apple’s Wearables, Home and Accessories unit still hauled $7.9 billion for the company in Q3 — putting it slightly behind Macs ($10.4 billion), slightly ahead of iPads ($6.2 billion), and contributing 7.6% of the company’s overall revenues for the quarter. With reportedly soft sales for the company’s latest iPhone and the big bet it’s placed on its soon-to-be-released foldable Duo not yet a surefire success, could the company’s new range of home products rise to the challenge and potentially help CEO John Ternus keep the Apple house in order? body_text: Somewhere between the invention of the internet and the rise of Wi-Fi, someone decided pigeons might be useful again. Back in 2001, Norwegian tech enthusiasts experimented with transmitting internet data via carrier pigeons. Of the nine packets sent, only four replies came back. Not exactly a technological breakthrough. But 25 years later, one of those packets is up for auction at Christie's , with bidding already reaching $4,000. Apparently, even a failed technology venture can appreciate in value. Stocks slid on Tuesday as US crude oil prices ticked higher while the global benchmark dropped. Bumble, the long-struggling dating app, has spent the past five years looking for love in a hopeless place: the Nasdaq stock exchange. The company announced Tuesday that Ithaca Holdings , an investment firm founded by two Silicon Valley veterans that appears to be less than a year old, has agreed to buy it for $1.3 billion cash in a take-private deal. Shareholders will receive $6.05 per share, a whopping 138% premium to Friday's closing price, the last trading day before the Wall Street Journal reported Bumble and Ithaca were in advanced talks. The $1.3 billion price tag may sound like a lot until you remember the company had a peak valuation of about $14 billion around the time it went public in 2021. Bumble has seen its sales decline for the past few years and is expected to report a $15 million net loss for this fiscal year which would mark its fifth consecutive year in the red. It’s unclear exactly how Ithaca plans to turn it around. In a statement, Bumble CEO Whitney Wolfe Herd (who, notably, recused herself from the board vote on the takeover) said Ithaca is “a partner who shares our vision, believes in our women-first mission, and is committed to investing in Bumble’s future.” In case you forgot: Wolfe Herd founded Bumble as a women-focused dating app in 2014, she announced she was stepping down as CEO in 2023, then returned in 2025. Bumble — not unlike its peer apps owned by Match Group — has struggled to keep users engaged, particularly younger ones who are growing tired of endless swiping. Its paying user base shrank 16% year-over-year to 3.2 million in the second quarter , while revenue fell about 15%. The company has been trying to reinvent itself, loosening its signature women-make-the-first-move rule and experimenting with in-person events where users meet before matching. Its biggest planned change is doing away with the swipe altogether, although it hasn't revealed what will replace it. The new model is expected to begin rolling out in early 2027, following technical delays. The takeover also means a changing of the guard: Ithaca founders Ravi Gupta, a former Instacart executive, and John Hegeman, a former Meta executive, will become Bumble's co-CEOs. Wolfe Herd will remain involved with the company she founded. You need a big enough pool of people on your platform. Then you have to convince enough of those people to pay for premium features. And then, if those premium features actually work, you’re perpetually cannibalizing your own subscriber base. Not to mention the tides are turning away from swipe-based apps. Gen Z would rather touch grass and seek a meet-cute than brainrot on a dating app. While some startups are certainly trying , It’s unclear where Bumble or its peers squeeze shareholder value from in that world. 📊 Inflation: There’s a 50% chance that inflation comes in above 3.6% in September, according to prediction markets, with an 8% chance that it comes in even hotter at 3.7%. 🏛️ Senate: On a related note, we are now just three weeks out from the midterms, and markets are pricing in a blue wave. title: ⛽ A diesel deal
body_text: Seven masked thieves pulled off an audacious heist at Tuscan warehouse, expertly disabling the alarm system before carting away 30,000 bottles of rare wine, the Financial Times reports . The wine, made by family owned Marchesi Antinori, which traces its history back to 1385, sell from between about $170 and $560 a bottle. The thieves seemed to have intimate knowledge of the specialized storage facility’s operations, with the robbery timed just before Antinori was about to send out consignment shipments to some of its best customers, ensuring the warehouse would be laden with valuable bottles. It’s the most recent in a string of thefts in Italy targeting high-end wine in storage or at restaurant cellars. Antinori says it went public with the sale in the hope that enterprising oenophiles can be on the lookout for the looted bottles. When we last checked in on the White House’s attempts to get the price of diesel down, the President was floating the idea of allowing red dye diesel – which is chemically identical to normal diesel but with added red dye and is exempt from federal taxes but restricted to off-road vehicles – to be used for to be used for normal on-road uses. Energy experts doubted the policy change would do much to push prices downward, and would likely result in red dye diesel becoming more expensive, putting even greater cost pressure on farmers. Now, the White House is trying a different approach: get Russia back into the (legal) petroleum products exports business. On Friday, the Trump administration announced that the US will buy 36 million barrels of Russian diesel over the next several months, with 2.25 million barrels purchased immediately. Prices did initially tick down on the news, but the challenge is the context: the world uses around 30 million barrels of diesel per day. US truckers use almost 3 million barrels of diesel a day, Reuters reports . The news agency pointed out that the shipments of Russian diesel that the US has announced a schedule for thus far amount to less than four days of what US trucks use daily. The Financial Times noted that industry analysts expected the deal to have very little impact on global supplies and thus prices. President Trump went further on Sunday evening, announcing a so-called energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in which both nations would abstain from attacking energy infrastructure. Shortly after the announcement, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia carried out a target strike in violation of the ceasefire. Both the international and US benchmarks for crude oil prices rose a little over 2% on Monday. Attempting to use Russian imports to drive down diesel prices is a tenuous tactic given the scale of the shipments announced thus far, and, as Deutsche Bank’s Jim Reid told the FT, the uncertainty of any truce between the Kremlin and Ukraine. But as long as diesel prices stay elevated, expect more policy activity from the White House. “There is a lot of impetus to do more,” Citigroup ’s head of energy strategy Anthony Yuen pointed out , because GOP districts “tend to consume more diesel”.
